On this day in 45 BC, the Julian calendar instituted by the first Roman emperor, Julius Caesar, officially took effect with
January 1st marking the beginning of the year in ancient Rome
and, eventually, much of the world. The Julian calendar did away with the Roman habit of adding an additional month from time to time to make up for the drift inherent in a lunar calendar, instead instituting leap years every four years to keep the calendar stable. (Many centuries later, in 1752, the Gregorian calendar was developed to adjust for a remaining 11 minutes of drift that had not been understood by the ancient Romans. The Gregorian calendar does away with leap years at the turn of the century, except in years divisible by 400.)
